title: RSI Divergence: How to Spot Bullish, Bearish and Hidden Divergence (With a Nifty Example)
summary: RSI divergence shows when price and momentum disagree. Learn the 4 types, how to confirm a signal on Nifty, and how to backtest it without coding.
body_markdown:
RSI divergence is when price and the Relative Strength Index (RSI) move in opposite directions. Price makes a new high or low, but RSI does not confirm it. This shows the momentum behind the move is fading, which often comes before a reversal or a pause.


There are four types: regular bullish, regular bearish, hidden bullish and hidden bearish. Regular divergence warns that a trend may reverse. Hidden divergence suggests the trend is likely to continue.


Divergence is a warning sign, not a buy or sell button. This guide shows how to spot each type, confirm it, and check whether it actually worked on Nifty before you put money on it.

## What Is RSI? A Quick Refresher


RSI is a momentum indicator created by J. Welles Wilder. It measures how fast and how strongly price has moved over a set number of candles, usually 14.


RSI moves between 0 and 100:


-


A reading above 70 is usually treated as overbought.


-


A reading below 30 is usually treated as oversold.


-


The 50 level acts as the line between bullish and bearish momentum.


Think of RSI as a speedometer and price as the road. A car can keep climbing a hill while it slows down. Divergence is when you notice the speedometer dropping even though the car is still climbing.


This early warning is a big reason RSI ranks among the[best indicators for intraday trading](https://algotest.in/blog/5-best-indicators-for-intraday-trading/) . Here is an easy way to remember the difference. In regular divergence, price makes the more extreme point. In hidden divergence, RSI makes the more extreme point.


### Regular Bullish Divergence (Positive Divergence)


Price makes a lower low, but RSI makes a higher low. Sellers pushed price lower, but with less force than before.


It usually appears near the end of a downtrend and can come before a bounce.


### Regular Bearish Divergence (Negative Divergence)


Price makes a higher high, but RSI makes a lower high. Buyers are still pushing price up, but each push is weaker.


Traders often use it as a cue to book profits on long trades or to prepare for a fall.


### Hidden Bullish Divergence


Price makes a higher low, but RSI makes a lower low. This shows up during a pullback in an uptrend.


Price held above its old low even though momentum dipped deeper. That is a sign buyers are still in control.


### Hidden Bearish Divergence


Price makes a lower high, but RSI makes a higher high. It forms during a bounce inside a downtrend.


Price failed to reach its old high even though momentum rose. That is a sign sellers still have the upper hand.


## How to Spot RSI Divergence in 5 Steps


1.


**Add RSI (14) below your price chart.** For intraday trading, start with a 15-minute chart. Very short charts like 1 or 3 minutes show divergence every few candles, and most of it means little. This guide on the[best time frame for intraday trading](https://algotest.in/blog/best-time-frame-for-intraday-trading/) can help you pick one.


2.


**Mark two clear swing points on price.** Use two swing lows for bullish divergence and two swing highs for bearish divergence. A common rule of thumb is to keep them at least 5 candles apart and within about 50 to 60 candles.


3.


**Read RSI on the same two candles.** Do not use the nearest RSI peak. Use the RSI value on the exact candles where price made its swing.


4.


**Compare the direction.** Draw one line connecting the two price points and another connecting the two RSI points. If the lines slope in opposite directions, you have divergence.


5.


**Check where RSI is.** Bullish divergence carries more weight when the first RSI low is below 30. Bearish divergence carries more weight when the first RSI high is above 70.


## RSI Divergence Example on Nifty


The numbers below are illustrative. They show how to read the setup on a 15-minute Nifty chart.


**Bullish divergence:**


-


Nifty falls to 24,800 and RSI drops to 22, deep in oversold territory.


-


Price bounces to 24,950.


-


Nifty falls again to 24,720, a lower low, but this time RSI only drops to 29, a higher low.


-


Price made a new low with weaker selling behind it, which is regular bullish divergence.


What a trader might do next:


-


A cautious trader waits for a 15-minute close above 24,950, the bounce high between the two lows.


-


A faster trader enters when RSI crosses back above 30 and accepts more false signals in return.


-


In both cases, the stop loss sits just below 24,720, because a break of that low means the divergence has failed.


**Bearish divergence:**


-


Nifty rises to 25,600 with RSI at 74.


-


Price dips to 25,480 and then climbs to 25,660, a higher high.


-


RSI only reaches 63 on the second high, a lower high.


-


This is not an instant short signal, but it tells you the rally is losing strength, so it is a good time to tighten stops on long trades and watch for a break below 25,480.


## How to Confirm RSI Divergence Before You Trade


In a strong trend, divergence can show up two or three times before price actually turns. Every early entry can cost you, so wait for at least one confirmation:


-


A close above the swing high between the two lows confirms a bullish divergence, and a close below the swing low between the two highs confirms a bearish one.


-


RSI crossing back above 30 ([bullish](https://algotest.in/blog/automate-your-bullish-engulf-using-chartink-and-algotest) ) or below 70 ([bearish](https://algotest.in/blog/bearish-candle) ) shows momentum is really turning, and some traders wait for a cross of 50 for stronger proof.


-


When[ADX](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-automate-adx-indicator/) is above 25 and rising, the trend is strong, so treat regular divergence against that trend with extra caution.


-


A close back above a short[EMA](https://algotest.in/blog/automate-ema-indicator-without-coding/) , such as the 20 EMA, adds weight to a bullish divergence.


-


Divergence that forms near support, resistance or the outer[Bollinger Bands](https://algotest.in/blog/bollinger-bands-strategies-for-indian-traders/) means more than one that forms in the middle of a range.

Hidden divergence works better as a re-entry tool. In an uptrend, a hidden bullish divergence with RSI holding in the 40 to 50 zone can mark the end of a pullback. In a downtrend, look for hidden bearish divergence with RSI stalling around 50 to 60.


## Common RSI Divergence Mistakes


-


Trading against a strong trend is the most common error, because RSI can stay overbought or oversold for hours while divergence keeps printing.


-


Reading RSI on the wrong candle creates false divergence, so always use the RSI value on the exact swing candles.


-


Mixing up regular and hidden divergence can make you trade a reversal when the chart is pointing to continuation.


-


Using 1-minute or 3-minute charts gives you divergence every few candles, and most of it is noise.


-


Holding on after price breaks the second swing low or high turns a small loss into a big one, because the setup is already invalid.


-


Trading divergence on event days like RBI policy or the Union Budget is risky, since price gaps can jump right past your levels.


-


Trusting a setup because it looked right on a few charts is not enough, so test it on past data and practise on[paper trading websites](https://algotest.in/blog/paper-trading-websites-india/) before going live.

### FAQs


#### Is RSI divergence a reliable signal?


It is a useful early warning, but it is not reliable on its own. Divergence can repeat several times in a strong trend before price turns. It works better with a confirmation, such as a price break or an RSI cross, and after you have tested it on past data.


#### What is the best timeframe for RSI divergence?


For intraday trading, 15-minute and 1-hour charts give cleaner divergences than 1-minute or 5-minute charts. Swing traders often use daily charts. Higher timeframes give fewer signals, but each one tends to matter more.


#### What is the best RSI setting for divergence?


RSI 14 is the standard setting and works well for most traders. Some intraday traders use RSI 9 or 10 for faster signals, which also brings more noise. Whatever you choose, keep it the same across all your tests.


#### What is the difference between regular and hidden divergence?


Regular divergence compares the extremes of a move and warns that the trend may turn. Hidden divergence compares the pullbacks inside a trend and suggests the trend will resume. Most traders use regular divergence for reversal trades and hidden divergence for re-entries.


#### What is positive and negative divergence in RSI?


Positive divergence is another name for bullish divergence, where price makes a lower low while RSI makes a higher low. Negative divergence is bearish divergence, where price makes a higher high while RSI makes a lower high.


#### Is RSI divergence better than MACD divergence?


Neither is better in every market. RSI reacts faster and has fixed 0 to 100 levels, so overbought and oversold zones are easy to read. MACD is smoother and slower, so it tends to give fewer but later signals. Some traders wait for both to agree.


#### Can you automate an RSI divergence strategy?


Yes. You can turn divergence into rules using RSI and candle values from earlier candles, then connect those rules to a trading strategy. AlgoTest lets you backtest, forward test and run such a rule live through your broker without coding.
